prompt: Build the signup page for a meal-planning app called Plateful: name, email, password, how many people they cook for, and a terms checkbox. Show the page as it looks right after someone pressed the button with a couple of mistakes, so I can see how the errors look.
prompt_suffix: Return the result as a single self-contained HTML file: all CSS inline, no external requests, system fonts only. Reply with one ```html fenced block and nothing else.
rubric: Every field has a visible label that stays on screen, not a placeholder standing in for a label.
Each error message sits next to the field it belongs to, says in plain words what to fix, and does not rely on colour alone.
What the person already typed is kept, and the password requirements are visible without having to fail first.
The form is a single clear column with one primary button and a sensible order and grouping of fields.
Inputs are easy to see and use: visible borders, comfortable height and legible text size.
featuring_rule: Declared before any run: rank the 3 without-skill runs and the 3 with-skill runs separately by the blind judge's rubric mean (two passes with the sides swapped, scores averaged), and feature the median run of each arm. The best run is never chosen. The contact sheet shows all six runs.

pairs.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep labels visible, keep what the person typed, put errors right under their fields with an icon, and use a single column with one primary button. B's error messages are more specific ('Enter an email address with an @'), its password requirement sits above the field before anyone types, and it adds a Show toggle and helper text explaining why the people count is asked. A's input borders are faint and pinkish, so its fields are harder to see. B's screenshot cuts off the button at the bottom, which is a minor flaw. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages keep visible labels, keep what the person typed, and show errors with icons next to the right field. A is a bit stronger: its error messages are more specific, the error summary repeats the actual fixes, the password rule sits above the field with a Show toggle, and the input borders are clearly visible. B is clean and well ordered, but its input borders are faint, its password hint is small and placed below the field, and its email error is more generic.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A shows the whole page, including the terms checkbox and its error, the one primary button and the login link. Every error has an icon and a plain fix right below its field, and the password rule shows without having to fail first. B's error details are a bit stronger: the password rule sits above the field, errors start with 'Error:', there's a Show toggle, and it says 'Yours has 7'. But the screenshot is cut off before the terms checkbox and the submit button, so I couldn't check its layout and button, which costs it on item 4. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A's screenshot is cut off after the household-size field, so its terms checkbox, terms error and primary button never appear, even though the request was to see how the errors look. What A does show is strong: the password requirements sit above the field, and each error has an icon, an 'Error:' prefix and very specific wording. B shows the complete form in one clean column, with errors next to each field, an icon and plain wording. Its password hint is small and sits below the input, but it is visible before any failure.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B shows the password rule ('At least 8 characters') before anyone gets it wrong, and its error messages start with 'Error:' and an icon, so they don't rely on colour. A's form is polished and fully visible, but you only learn the 10-character password rule after failing. B's screenshot cuts off before the submit button, so its layout can't be fully checked. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers have persistent labels, errors placed under the right fields with icons and plain wording, kept input values and clear bordered inputs. A shows the password rule ('At least 8 characters') before anyone fails it, while B only reveals the 10-character minimum in the error after submission. However, A's primary button is cut off in the screenshot, while B shows the complete form with one clear button.
